title: Human-AI decisions: Self-knowledge conditions unrealized gains
desc: Shows case uncertainty and model error can reverse assistance benefits, favouring workflow experiments over routine deployment.

kps.k: Strong standalone AI performance does not guarantee better human–AI decisions.
kps.d: The cluster distinguishes model accuracy, observed assistance effects and hypothetical gains from combining information. In Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence, CheXpert achieves an AUC of 0.85 and exceeds 78% of sampled radiologists; a fitted combined-signal benchmark reaches 0.88. Yet actual AI access produces no significant average diagnostic improvement and increases assessment time by about 4%. The ABC's image-prediction experiment instead finds average accuracy gains. These contrasting results make complementarity an empirical question about the task and interaction, rather than an automatic consequence of a capable model.

qs.q: First, we see that AI with an AUC of 0.85 is more accurate than 78% of humans, which means that a majority of radiologists would do better by simply following the AI prediction.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: We find that AI assistance improves prediction accuracy on average and with heteroge- neous impacts across individuals.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Who benefits depends on more than baseline skill or seniority; self-calibration offers a conditional explanation.
kps.d: Yu and colleagues analyze 140 radiologists across 15 diagnostic tasks and find individual benefits and harms, even after shrinking estimates to reduce sampling-error inflation. Experience, thoracic specialization, AI familiarity and baseline skill predict incremental gains poorly, challenging earlier reported experience associations. By contrast, The ABC's finds that low-ability participants with well-calibrated beliefs about their own ability gain most: holding ability fixed, a one-standard-deviation increase in calibration corresponds to a 20% larger assistance effect. This does not establish a universal low-performer advantage. Yu and colleagues also distinguish predicting assisted performance from predicting improvement and use separate case samples to avoid spurious baseline–gain relationships.

qs.q: Empirical Bayes for individual heterogeneity We used the empirical Bayes method 30 to shrink the raw mean heterogeneous treatment effects and performance metrics of individual radiologists measured on the dataset toward the grand mean to ameliorate overestimating heterogeneity due to sampling error.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Holding baseline ability fixed, a one standard deviation increase in calibration increases the average treatment e↵ect of AI assistance by 20 percent.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Case-level uncertainty and AI error can turn assistance from helpful to harmful.
kps.d: Combining Human Expertise finds that assistance helps when radiologists are uncertain but harms when they confidently rule out pathology; it helps when AI strongly predicts absence but harms in its uncertain middle range. Sparse high-probability cases limit conclusions elsewhere. Yu and colleagues find that AI errors below 20 associate with a 0.679-point improvement in absolute probability error, while errors above 80 associate with a −16.845-point effect on the 0–100 scale. However, relationships reverse for some pathologies, remain unclear for others and do not yield a clear overall AUROC trend. Underestimation also associates with better aggregate effects than equally large overestimation. AI confidence, actual error and human confidence therefore require separate analysis.

qs.q: The results reveal that AI assistance improves performance on both metrics when radiologists express uncertainty, but harms performance when radiologists are highly confident that a pathology is absent.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: More accurate AI predictions led to higher treatment effects: AI assistance with absolute error under 20 resulted in a treatment effect of 0.679 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.492 to 0.865, n  = 176,130; Supplementary Table 11 ), whereas AI assistance with absolute error above 80 resulted in a treatment effect of −16.845 (95% CI: −24.288 to −9.403, n  = 371).
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The sources identify unrealized gains from combining information, but differ in how far they infer behavioral mechanisms.
kps.d: Combining Human Expertise shows that clinical history adds information unavailable to image-only AI and reduces deviation from the diagnostic standard by 4%. Its preferred descriptive model combines underweighting AI with neglecting dependence between human and AI signals; among the compared models, both errors are needed to reproduce deterioration with uncertain AI. That modeling was not preregistered and understates some observed magnitudes. Yu and colleagues explicitly decline to infer cognitive mechanisms because case characteristics confound AI-error relationships. The ABC's links self-miscalibration to limited equalization and estimates that eliminating it would nearly double the reduction in the interquartile performance gap, but this is a counterfactual, not a tested intervention.

qs.q: to clinical history reduces the deviation from the diagnostic standard by 4.0% (p < 0.05) of the control mean.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Therefore, these findings should not be extrapolated for defining the cognitive mechanism in which AI assistance helps or hurts radiologists.

kps.k: Practical recommendations favor testing alternative workflows rather than assuming routine assistance is optimal.
kps.d: Yu and colleagues recommend measuring each radiologist's response in realistic simulations representative of the target population, task and AI system. Combining Human Expertise models selective assignment to AI alone or unassisted humans, with few cases handled jointly, when minimizing diagnostic loss plus human time costs under zero marginal AI cost and observed behavior. This is a modeled allocation result, not a deployed clinical outcome: correct signal combination would make joint diagnosis optimal more often. Training, explanations and richer reports remain proposed improvements; the studies do not establish their effectiveness, and additional information may increase cognitive burden.

qs.q: Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.
qs.a: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists · Academia · 2024

qs.q: We assume that the AI signal can always be obtained at zero marginal cost and implement a classifier that decides, as a function of the AI prediction, to delegate a patient to either be diagnosed by a human, a human with access to the AI, or the AI alone.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Task-specific diagnostic results do not establish occupation-wide displacement or generalize directly to generative AI.
kps.d: The radiology experiments use historical chest X-rays and probability-based assistance; Combining Human Expertise measures agreement with an expert-derived diagnostic standard rather than patient outcomes and explicitly limits extrapolation to generative AI. Task substitution can coexist with complementarity across a broader job. The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce operationalizes this distinction by weighting interpretation work across modalities using study volumes, radiologist shares and work RVUs, while including pre-, intra- and post-procedure tasks. Its supplied excerpt reports methods, not workforce outcomes; the assumption that interpretation occupies 80% of time is a sensitivity test for academically weighted data, not a universal observation.

qs.q: We follow the machine learning literature (Sheng et al., 2008) and construct a diagnostic standard by aggregating the assessments of five board-certified radiologists practicing at a highly reputed hospital with at least ten years of experience and chest radiology as a sub-specialty.4 We also show that our results are robust to a host of alternative constructions of the diagnostic standard.
qs.a: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Because the effect of AI tools varies across imaging modalities, we estimated the fraction of time radiologists spend on interpreting studies from each modality based on the number of studies performed each year in the US [[17](#R17)–[22](#R22)], the percentage of those studies interpreted by radiologists, and a work RVU adjustment commonly used by radiology practice to measure productivity [[23](#R23)].
qs.a: The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce: A Task-Based Analysis · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources support the proposition that capable AI does not automatically improve human–AI decisions and that benefits depend on user calibration, case-level uncertainty, model error and deployment design. Experimental evidence supplies the common basis: one study finds self-calibration materially increases assistance gains; radiology studies find heterogeneous benefits and harms, including no significant average improvement despite strong standalone AI performance and substantial harm when predictions are badly wrong. These sources consequently favour empirical workflow testing, individualized assessment or selective assignment over routine joint use. Material internal variation remains. The calibration experiment reports positive average gains and identifies beliefs about one’s own ability as a conditioning factor, whereas one radiology experiment finds no significant average gain and advances a cautious, model-based account of signal-combination errors. Another radiology study declines to establish a cognitive mechanism and emphasizes task-, pathology- and metric-dependent heterogeneity. A workforce-analysis source redirects to a modality- and task-based framing spanning pre-, intra- and post-procedure work; it does not test the proposition’s decision-level mechanisms or report workforce outcomes. This assessment characterizes only the supplied curated sources, not academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that capable AI does not automatically produce better human–AI decisions and that gains depend on the user, case and workflow. Across the sources, the common explanation is heterogeneity: assistance can improve average performance in one task yet fail to improve it in another, while user calibration, human uncertainty and model error materially affect whether it helps or harms. The main internal variation concerns mechanism and deployment. The ABC’s experiment identifies self-calibration as a significant moderator and uses a counterfactual to estimate unrealized equalising gains. One radiology study instead finds no significant average improvement and models errors in combining human and AI signals, leading conditionally to selective assignment rather than routine joint diagnosis. The other radiology study documents substantial individual variation and recommends realistic, individualized deployment testing, but explicitly declines to infer a cognitive mechanism. These findings are task-specific: the radiology systems provide diagnostic probabilities rather than generative-AI output, and the evidence does not establish broad conclusions about generative AI or occupation-level effects.

elens.an: The 2025 source does not assess the proposition’s central claim that self-knowledge, case uncertainty and model error condition whether human–AI assistance improves decisions. It instead redirects the analysis toward adoption at scale through a task- and modality-specific framework for estimating workforce effects. Its reasoning is that AI’s impact varies across imaging modalities and may extend beyond image interpretation to pre-, intra- and post-procedure work. Material variation within the source concerns how radiologists’ time is allocated: the primary estimates are adjusted using procedure volumes, radiologist participation and work RVUs, while an alternative 80% interpretation-time assumption tests sensitivity to academically weighted data. Because the supplied excerpt presents methods and application categories rather than workforce outcomes, it neither confirms routine deployment benefits nor directly supports the proposition’s recommended workflow experiments.
